title: More-than visual approaches to architecture. Vision, touch, technique
central_proposition: To overcome the ocularcentric bias in architecture and geography, this paper advocates for a "more-than visual" approach to built spaces, emphasizing the integration of haptic, optic, and somatic sensory-somatic and affective experiences, and exploring how these are conceptualized and operationalized in design.

concept_definitions.name: More-than visual
concept_definitions.definition: An approach that attends to a range of sensory-somatic and affective experiences that include, but crucially are not limited to, the visual.

concept_definitions.name: Haptic system
concept_definitions.definition: An apparatus by which the individual gets information about both his environment and his body, allowing him to feel an object relative to the body and the body relative to an object, literally in touch with the environment.

concept_definitions.name: Somatic senses
concept_definitions.definition: A collective term for internally felt bodily sensations, including proprioception, kinaesthesia, and the vestibular system, which constitute background feelings of embodiment and self-perception of inner bodily states.

concept_definitions.name: Proprioception
concept_definitions.definition: The sense by which the body knows itself, judges with perfect, automatic and instantaneous precision the position and motion of all its movable parts, their relations to one another, and their alignment in space.

concept_definitions.name: Interoception
concept_definitions.definition: Inwardly felt bodily sensations distinct from exteroception or outwardly oriented perceptions.

concept_definitions.name: Tactile appropriation
concept_definitions.definition: A mode of experiencing architecture accomplished by habit, custom, or usage rather than rapt attention, which determines optical reception and collapses optical distance.

concept_definitions.name: Kinaesthetic empathy
concept_definitions.definition: A proprioceptive projection into the space of the built environment, responding to movement within buildings as an anticipative postural stance within the apprehension of a structure.

concept_definitions.name: Technē
concept_definitions.definition: The skills of the craftsman, relating to poiēsis or the creative capacity of the craftsman.

concept_definitions.name: Tektōn
concept_definitions.definition: Greek root for 'builder', related to the logic of the building process.

concept_definitions.name: Biogram
concept_definitions.definition: Lived diagrams, involuntary, subjectively-felt and dynamic 'event-perceptions combining senses, tenses and dimensions on a single surface', inherent in the process of perception.

argument_structure: The paper begins by critiquing the visual bias in architectural and geographical discourse, then historically recontextualizes "haptic sensibility" through art historical figures like Wölfflin and Benjamin, who explored the interplay of vision and touch. It then transitions to contemporary design, introducing concepts like "haptic diagrams" and "biograms" from Massumi and Spuybroek, to demonstrate how proprioceptive and kinaesthetic empathy can be integrated into architectural technique and design processes for a more embodied experience.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core mechanism involves the interaction and integration of multiple sensory systems (haptic, optic, somatic, proprioceptive, kinaesthetic, vestibular) to form a holistic, embodied experience of architectural space. This experience is not merely visual but involves muscular responses, balance, internal bodily states, and habitual interactions, which collectively shape affective and cognitive responses to the built environment. The "biogram" concept suggests that these multi-sensory, dynamic, and involuntary "event-perceptions" are inherent in perception and can be triggered by design.

findings.antecedent: Ocularcentric bias in architectural design and experience
findings.consequent: Marginalization of tectonic and tactile dimensions; architecture as 'stage sets for the eye' or 'retinal architecture'
findings.mechanism: A focus on light, surfaces, visually apprehended forms, and design technologies detaches construction from material realities, leading to a narrow sensory engagement.
findings.quote: the concentration of the play of light, surfaces and visually apprehended forms has furthered the ocularcentric approach to the design and experience of buildings in modernity.

findings.antecedent: Return to embodied spatial experience in architectural literature
findings.consequent: Broadly humanistic phenomenology in architectural thinking
findings.mechanism: Mobilization of figures like Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty, and Bachelard to articulate a humanist agenda that accommodates the significance of the senses and the centrality of embodiment.
findings.quote: What unites these figures throughout the decades is broadly a return to embodied spatial experience by means of a broadly humanistic phenomenology.

findings.consequent: Limited conceptions of the human body ('self-imaging')
findings.mechanism: Architects assume prospective inhabitants are proportioned exactly like themselves, an imaginative projection that ignores bodily difference or impairment.
findings.quote: Imrie (2003) found that the body is still ignored in (design) practice. Architects assumed the prospective inhabitants of their buildings to be proportioned exactly like themselves

findings.consequent: Suppression of visual image dominance; enhancement of plasticity, tactility, and intimacy
findings.mechanism: An unconscious element of touch is concealed within the sense of vision, where the eye 'touches' the object, determining its sensual quality and mediating messages of invitation or rejection.
findings.quote: The haptic sensibility suppresses the dominance of the visual image through enhancing plasticity, tactility and intimacy. An unconscious element of touch is unavoidably concealed in the sense of vision

findings.antecedent: Wölfflin's 'linear' mode of visuality (e.g., Dürer's draughtsmanship, classical architecture)
findings.consequent: Ocular-motor experience, physical grasping, tactile values, clear lines/edges, static representation
findings.mechanism: The operation of the eye in tracing figures with clear lines resembles the hand feeling along a body, and modelling repeats reality in light gradation, appealing to the sense of touch.
findings.quote: The tracing out of a figure with an evenly clear line has still an element of physical grasping. The operation which the eye performs resembles the operation of the hand which feels along the body

findings.antecedent: Wölfflin's 'painterly' mode of visuality (e.g., Rembrandt's painting, Baroque architecture)
findings.consequent: Exclusion of direct tactile analogy; roots only in the eye; indistinct patches, changing forms; withdrawal from tactile zone; more replete bodily involvement; proprioceptive response
findings.mechanism: This mode allows for a generalized sensory intermingling and validates the non-optical functions of the eye, leading to forms perceived as changing and invoking proprioceptive and more-than-visual responses.
findings.quote: A painterly representation, on the other hand, excludes this analogy. It has its roots only in the eye and appeals only to the eye... this involves more of the body than the eyes in forming affective response, invoking something more proprioceptive, and certainly more-than visual.

findings.antecedent: Physical forms of architecture (e.g., Baroque architecture with gravitas and weightiness)
findings.consequent: Affective response (corporeal and spiritual, heaviness of limbs, need to resist crumbling)
findings.mechanism: Our bodily organization conditions responses; we inevitably project our own bodily experiences (muscular contraction, responses to gravity) onto architectural forms.
findings.quote: 'Physical forms possess a character only because we ourselves possess a body', he says (1998: 712), and thus have such experiences as muscular contraction, responses to gravity and interactions with materials.

findings.antecedent: Habitual use and familiarity with architectural space
findings.consequent: Tactile appropriation; less distanced, abstract, or contemplative stance; influence on optical reception; collapse of optical distance
findings.mechanism: Appropriation occurs by habit, custom, or usage, rather than rapt attention, leading to an almost ineffable 'feel' of a building and a more proximal engagement.
findings.quote: Tactile appropriation is accomplished not so much by attention as by habit. As regards architecture, habit determines to a large extent even optical reception.

findings.antecedent: Architectural design (materials, structural forms, relative movements, speeds, stillnesses)
findings.consequent: Kinaesthetic empathy; proprioceptive projection; anticipative postural stance; evoked proprioceptive feelings; address to musculature
findings.mechanism: Buildings do not just imitate static proportions but also the mechanics of posture, expressing movement/stillness through the interplay of skeleton and musculature, becoming a language of potential movements and emotive states.
findings.quote: Like a proprioceptive projection into the space of the built environment, kinaesthetic empathy responds to movement within buildings, an anticipative postural stance within the apprehension of a structure.

findings.antecedent: Haptic engagement with diagrammatic tools (digital media) in architectural design
findings.consequent: Shift from 'representation' to 'operation' and from 'contemplation' to 'involvement'
findings.mechanism: Overcoming the precedence of optics by means of optical apparatuses themselves, mediated by technology, generates active involvement in the design process.
findings.quote: an overcoming of the precedence of ... optics by means of the optical apparatuses in themselves. Mediated by technology, the haptic has changed our way of operating in the world, generating a shift from contemplation alone to active involvement.

findings.antecedent: Wölfflin's linear style / rigid diagrammatic form in design
findings.consequent: Eyes follow clear linear forms; colour contrast accentuates; engagement of ocular-motor responses and saccades
findings.mechanism: The clear lines and edges of the linear style engage specific ocular-motor responses, leading to a distinct visual rhythm and scanning pattern.
findings.quote: the tactility of Wölfflin's linear style is comparable to the rigid diagrammatic form within the design stage, where eyes follow clearly linear forms and the colour contrast accentuates this

findings.antecedent: Wölfflin's painterly style / patches of colour in design
findings.consequent: Collective pull of multiple sensations; non-optical functions; synaesthetic interleaving (tactile, proprioceptive, kinaesthetic) through ocular means
findings.mechanism: Engagement with the rhythm and intensity of saccadic eye movements promotes associated movement, stillness, or rest, thereby activating and integrating multisensory systems.
findings.quote: the patches of colour of Wölfflin's painterly style perform a collective pull of multiple sensations through the non-optical functions, the larger optical apparatus, and is consequently always potentially synaesthetic in interleaving not just the tactile, but also the proprioceptive and the kinaesthetic, through ocular means.

findings.consequent: Mismatch with embodied haptic and optic experience; spatial experience sacrificed for geometric/geographical coherence
findings.mechanism: Plans are 'convenient fictions' that deny human binocular vision, saccadic visual reception, the curvature of the earth, and the effects of atmospheric distortion, leading to a discrepancy between abstract representation and lived experience.
findings.quote: The familiar but fundamental mismatch between an idealised plan and its real-world actualisation is applicable to the embodied haptic and optic experience of a building, considers Treib: ‘The plan gives us a coherent idea at the expense of spatial experience, and barters human experience for geo-metric or geographical coherence'

findings.consequent: Generative, incorporates specific information, unfolds complexity, offers potentials for movement, divergence, becomings, and affects
findings.mechanism: Operates as an 'abstract machine' (Deleuze) for distributing power to affect and be affected, and as a 'potent political device' (Vidler) entraining political vision within its form.
findings.quote: Instead, they 'operate as abstract machines for proliferation; they are generative; they incorporate specific information; and they unfold in their complexity'

findings.consequent: Spatial orientation, navigation, 'lived diagrams' (biograms), involuntary, dynamic, synaesthetic interaction between vision and proprioception
findings.mechanism: Proprioception is a 'self-referential' sense directly registering body displacements; orientation is a tropism (tendency + habit) rather than cognition (visual form + configuration); a synaesthetic system cross-references dual sense systems.
findings.quote: If the visual is an 'exoreferential' sense that supposedly refers beyond the body, then proprioception is a ‘self-referential' sense that 'directly registers displacements of the body relative to each other'

findings.antecedent: Biograms (inherent in perception, can be remarked/transposed/redescribed)
findings.consequent: Architectural design process incorporating 'biogrammatic triggers or elicitation devices'; proprioceptive and more-than-visual design
findings.mechanism: Biograms embed logics of perception and experience into modeling, allowing designers to think about material, weight, sensations, and the deployment of light, textures, materials, reflectivity, and acoustics.
findings.quote: Massumi posits biograms as a favoured alternative to diagrams in the design process, embedding logics of perception and experience into the modelling process. Proprioceptive habits literally have weight, are incorporated into ‘visualisation' within design.

findings.consequent: Categorization, graphing, and representation of sensory properties of materials and spatial structures; charting complex sensory-spatial situations
findings.mechanism: An eight-fold breakdown (vision, sound, odour, four haptic subtypes) with perceived intensity mapped allows for analytical charting and potential interchange between architectural plan and technique.
findings.quote: Malnar and Vodvarka (2004) pursue an allied project, proposing a series of design resources for categorising, graphing and representing the sensory properties of a variety of materials and spatial structures.

findings.antecedent: Interwoven horizon of hapto-kinetic diagram and biogram, combined with historical concepts of proprioceptive projection and kinaesthetic empathy
findings.consequent: Different intuition of the relationship between inside/outside, intensity/extensity, haptic/optic; a more-than-visual experience of architecture
findings.mechanism: This integration overcomes rigid distinctions (interoception/exteroception), reveals the topological folding of the body's interior, and allows enculturated/accreted proprioceptive habits to determine movements and responses.
findings.quote: Through the interwoven horizon of the hapto-kinetic diagram and biogram, the associated historical concepts of proprioceptive projection and kinaesthetic empathy, we achieve a different intuition of the relationship between inside and outside, intensity and extensity, haptic and optic, each being aspects of a more-than visual experience of architectural spaces.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Architectural designs that explicitly incorporate "biogrammatic triggers" for multisensory (haptic, proprioceptive, kinaesthetic, visual) engagement will lead to a more immersive and affectively rich user experience compared to designs focused solely on visual aesthetics.

Users navigating spaces designed with a "painterly" aesthetic (emphasizing indistinct forms, patches of color, and multisensory pull) will exhibit different eye-tracking patterns and report higher levels of synaesthetic experience and embodied affect compared to spaces designed with a "linear" aesthetic (clear lines, distinct forms, tactile values).

Habitual interaction with a built environment will lead to a stronger "tactile appropriation," influencing optical perception and reducing perceived spatial distance, as measured by behavioral observation and self-report.

Designs that consider the "mechanics of posture" and evoke "kinaesthetic empathy" will elicit specific physiological (e.g., muscle tension, balance) and self-reported emotional responses related to movement and stillness.
The use of "sensory sliders" in the design process will lead to architectural outcomes that are perceived as more multisensorially coherent and affectively engaging by users.
bridge_warrants: Connects art history (Wölfflin, Benjamin) to architectural theory and design practice.
Links phenomenology (Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty, Bachelard) to critical geography and architectural experience, while also critiquing its 'unreconstructed humanism'.
Integrates concepts from neurophysiology (somatic senses, kinaesthesia, proprioception, saccades, synaesthesia) into architectural discourse.
Applies Deleuzian 'diagram' and Massumi's 'biogram' to architectural design as generative tools for 'more-than visual' experience.
methodological_critiques: Critiques humanistic geography and early phenomenology for being 'retrograde' and unable to address specificities of diverse bodily experiences (gendered, impaired, queer bodies).
Critiques architects' 'self-imaging' as a limited conception of the human body in design.
Critiques the 'dominant retinal architecture' and 'hegemony of the eye' in architecture.
Critiques the 'anecdotal, biographical and largely sentimental' approach in art historical teaching.
Critiques the 'fundamental mismatch between an idealised plan and its real-world actualisation' in architecture.
model_structure: The paper proposes a conceptual framework for understanding and designing architectural spaces, shifting from a purely visual, representational paradigm to a "more-than visual," operational, and embodied one. In this framework, "biograms" act as dynamic, multisensory event-perceptions that can be triggered by design. The framework emphasizes the interplay of haptic, optic, and somatic senses, mediated by technique (technē, tektōn), to shape embodied experience and affect.
limitations: Pallasmaa's phenomenological architecture is critiqued as 'domesticating, self-satisfied subjectivism-in-spite-of-itself' and returning 'home', implying a limitation in its scope or critical depth.

Malnar and Vodvarka's 'sensory sliders' are noted to 'perhaps too neatly it remains within the realm of a standardised representational repertoire,' suggesting a limitation in fully capturing the dynamic, subjective nature of biograms.
